lessons.title: How a Request Travels
lessons.summary: Follow a page load from the browser to the server and back.

sections.title: Start with a page load
sections.body:
You open a book’s page in an online store. The browser must find the server, connect to it, and request the page.

Assume the browser has no cached DNS answer and must open a new connection.
sections.visualNote: The first visit starts with an empty browser cache and no open connection.

sections.title: Find the address
sections.body: The browser resolves the store’s domain name to an IP address. If it has no valid answer in its cache, it asks a DNS resolver. The resolver can use its own cache or query other DNS servers.
sections.note: The time to live (TTL) tells a cache how long it can reuse a DNS answer.
sections.visualNote: The DNS reply gives the browser an address. The resolver can answer from its own cache.

sections.title: Open a secure connection
sections.body:
For this example, the browser opens a TCP connection to the server and starts a TLS handshake. During the handshake, the browser checks the server’s certificate and both sides establish encryption keys.

These exchanges take time before the first HTTP request. The browser can often reuse the connection for later requests.
sections.note: A round trip includes the time for a message to reach the server and for a reply to return.
sections.visualNote: This example uses TCP and TLS. Connection setup comes before the HTTP request.

sections.title: Send the HTTP request
sections.body: The browser asks for the book page with an HTTP GET request. The server reads the requested path and routes the request to the code that handles product pages.
sections.visualNote: The request path tells the server which book page to build.

sections.title: Read the product data
sections.body: The application asks the database for the book’s title, price, and stock status. The database returns the matching record. The application uses it to build the page.
sections.visualNote: The database sends the product record to the application.

sections.title: Receive the response
sections.body: The server sends an HTTP status, response headers, and the HTML. As the browser receives the HTML, it can start parsing it and find other files to fetch.
sections.visualNote: The response path runs from the application back to the browser.

sections.title: Load the other files
sections.body:
The HTML refers to a stylesheet, scripts, and a cover image. The browser can use cached copies when they are still valid and request the remaining files. A single page load can include many HTTP requests.

The diagram shows a file request to the store’s server. Some sites serve these files from a separate host.
sections.visualNote: The browser can request several page resources over the existing connection.

sections.title: Diagnose a slow database query
sections.body: The browser connects quickly, but the server spends most of the request time looking up the book. A server trace can show the database call and its duration. The database query plan can show how the database searched for the row.
sections.note: An index on a frequently queried field can reduce lookup time. Check the query plan and measure the result.
sections.visualNote: Inspect the database part of the trace before adding application servers.

sections.title: Compare users in different regions
sections.body:
A visitor far from the server can wait longer even when the server does the same work. Each network round trip adds delay. Compare request timings from two regions to see how much of the difference comes from the network.

A content delivery network can serve eligible files from a location closer to the visitor.
sections.visualNote: A distant visitor pays the extra delay on each network round trip.

sections.title: Review the timing
sections.body: Compare DNS lookup time, connection setup, time to the first response byte, and download time. Browser timings show what the visitor waits for. Server traces help explain the part spent in the application and database.
sections.note: Repeat the measurement with a warm cache and an existing connection. The browser can skip some of the work from the first load.
sections.visualNote: Compare a first visit with a repeat visit to see which work the browser can skip.

lessons.title: Latency & Throughput
lessons.summary: Separate how long one request takes from how much work a system handles.

sections.title: Measure latency
sections.body: Latency is the time taken for one operation. Percentiles show the experience of slow requests better than an average alone.
sections.visualNote: In this example, about 95% of requests finish within 120 ms. Check the slowest requests separately.

sections.title: Measure throughput
sections.body: Throughput is the number of operations completed per unit of time. A system can have high throughput while individual requests are slow.
sections.visualNote: Count requests that finish in the interval. Pending requests still occupy capacity.

sections.title: Find the bottleneck
sections.body: As utilization approaches capacity, queues can grow and tail latency can rise. Measure both throughput and latency under load.
sections.visualNote: If throughput stops rising under added load, look for the component where requests wait.

lessons.title: Napkin Math
lessons.summary: Estimate traffic, storage, and bandwidth before choosing a design.

sections.title: Estimate traffic
sections.body: Start with daily active users and requests per user. Divide daily requests by 86,400 to estimate average requests per second.
sections.visualNote: Divide by 86,400 seconds per day. This example assumes traffic is averaged over a full day.

sections.title: Allow for peaks
sections.body: Average traffic hides bursts. State a peak multiplier and calculate capacity for that load, then validate it with measurements.
sections.visualNote: The peak factor is an assumption. Replace it with traffic data when you have it.

sections.title: Estimate storage
sections.body: Multiply records per day by bytes per record and retention days. Include replication and index overhead in the estimate.
sections.visualNote: This example excludes indexes, replicas, and backups. Add their capacity separately.

lessons.title: Vertical vs Horizontal
lessons.summary: Choose between a larger machine and more machines.

sections.title: Scale up
sections.body: Vertical scaling gives one machine more CPU, memory, or storage. It is simple but limited by machine size and often needs downtime.
sections.visualNote: Add capacity to the existing server when the workload benefits from a larger machine.

sections.title: Scale out
sections.body: Horizontal scaling adds instances and distributes work between them. It adds coordination and operational complexity.
sections.visualNote: Both instances need to be able to process the requests sent to them.

sections.title: Choose for the bottleneck
sections.body: Measure the constrained resource first. Consider cost, failure recovery, data partitioning, and the speed at which capacity must change.
sections.visualNote: Compare the cost and recovery impact before you choose how to scale.

lessons.title: Load Balancing
lessons.summary: Distribute requests across healthy instances.

sections.title: Find the overloaded server
sections.body: A ticket site has two application servers. Clients use the address of Server A, so it receives all incoming requests. Server A starts to queue requests while Server B has capacity to help.
sections.visualNote: Server B has spare capacity, but every client connects to Server A.

sections.title: Give clients one service address
sections.body:
A load balancer receives requests at the public address of the service. For each request, it selects a backend server, forwards the request, and relays the response.

The client uses the same service address when the team adds, removes, or replaces a backend.
sections.note: A backend pool is the group of servers to which the load balancer can send traffic.
sections.visualNote: Publish the balancer address so backend addresses can change independently.

sections.title: Take turns with round robin
sections.body: Round robin cycles through the available servers in order. With two servers, it sends one request to Server A, the next to Server B, and then starts again at Server A.
sections.note: This policy works best when servers have similar capacity and requests take a similar amount of work.
sections.visualNote: A and B take turns receiving new work when both are available.

sections.title: Compare short and long requests
sections.body: Opening a ticket listing is fast. Generating a sales report takes longer. Both count as one request, but the report can hold resources for much longer. Equal request counts can therefore produce uneven server load.
sections.visualNote: Equal request counts can leave one server busier when request costs differ.

sections.title: Use the number of open connections
sections.body: Least connections sends a new connection to the server with the fewest open connections. If Server A still has many connections open while it runs reports, the load balancer can direct new connections to Server B.
sections.note: Open connections approximate load. One connection can carry multiple requests, so actual server load can differ.
sections.visualNote: The example favors Server B because it has fewer open connections.

sections.title: Route around an unhealthy server
sections.body: The load balancer checks whether each backend can serve traffic. When Server B fails enough checks to meet the configured threshold, the load balancer stops sending it new requests. Successful checks can return it to the pool.
sections.note: The remaining servers need enough capacity to handle the traffic after a backend fails.
sections.visualNote: Remove Server B from rotation after it fails the health check threshold.

sections.title: Check what happens when the balancer fails
sections.body: The load balancer is now on every request path. If it is the only one and it fails, both application servers can still be healthy while clients lose access to the service.
sections.visualNote: Both backends can still be healthy while the public entry point is down.

sections.title: Prepare a standby load balancer
sections.body:
Run a second balancer with the same routing rules. Keep it in a separate failure domain so a single host or network failure is less likely to stop both. The application servers still form one backend pool.

The diagram groups the public entry point into one node. In this arrangement, the active balancer handles the traffic while the standby waits.
sections.visualNote: The entry-point node represents the pair. Put the standby in a separate failure domain.

sections.title: Test the switch to standby
sections.body: When failure detection triggers a switch, the standby takes over the service address or a routing service sends traffic to it. New requests can reach the same healthy backends through the standby.
sections.note: Measure the switch time and the effect on open connections. Some clients may need to reconnect.
sections.visualNote: Measure how long the public address takes to work again after failover.

sections.title: Route by HTTP path
sections.body: An HTTP load balancer can select a backend pool using a request path. For example, requests for listings can go to a low-latency pool and requests for reports can go to a pool sized for longer jobs. In the diagram, each server represents one pool.
sections.visualNote: The two backend nodes now represent separate pools selected by the request path.

sections.title: Update one server at a time
sections.body: Before you update Server B, stop sending new traffic to it and allow active work to finish. Server A handles new traffic during the update. Return Server B to the pool after it passes its readiness checks.
sections.note: Check that Server A has enough capacity before taking Server B out of rotation.
sections.visualNote: Send new requests to Server A while Server B finishes existing requests.

sections.title: Review the request path
sections.body: Clients use one service address. The load balancer selects a healthy backend according to the routing policy. Backend health checks, balancer redundancy, and controlled deployments address different causes of interrupted service.
sections.visualNote: Test backend failure and load balancer failure as separate cases.

lessons.title: Stateless Services
lessons.summary: Make requests portable across service instances.

sections.title: Keep requests independent
sections.body: A stateless service does not depend on local session state from a previous request. Any healthy instance can handle the next request.
sections.visualNote: A second request can go to a different server from the first.

sections.title: Move shared state
sections.body: Store durable or shared session data in a database or shared cache. Protect it with suitable expiration and access controls.
sections.visualNote: Expire shared session records when the application no longer needs them.

sections.title: Scale and replace
sections.body: Instances can be added or replaced more easily, but the shared store must still handle load and failures.
sections.visualNote: Adding service replicas can increase load on the shared store.

lessons.title: Caching
lessons.summary: Serve repeated reads faster while managing stale data.

sections.title: Read through a cache
sections.body: A service checks the cache first. On a miss, it reads the source of truth and stores the result for later requests.
sections.visualNote: A miss fills the cache. A later hit can use that value without a database read.

sections.title: Set freshness rules
sections.body: Expiration limits how long a value stays cached. Invalidation can refresh data sooner but adds complexity and race conditions.
sections.visualNote: Set the lifetime from the amount of stale data a reader can accept.

sections.title: Handle misses safely
sections.body: A popular key expiring can send many requests to the database at once. Use request coalescing or staggered expiration when needed.
sections.visualNote: Coalescing lets requests for the same missing key share one database query.

lessons.title: Content Delivery
lessons.summary: Place static content closer to users.

sections.title: Serve from the edge
sections.body: A content delivery network caches eligible responses at locations near users, reducing distance and origin traffic.
sections.visualNote: A fresh public asset can leave the edge without a trip to the origin.

sections.title: Fetch on a miss
sections.body: When an edge has no fresh copy, it requests the content from the origin and may cache the response.
sections.visualNote: The edge can keep an eligible origin response for the next visitor.

sections.title: Control freshness
sections.body: Cache headers, versioned asset names, and invalidation determine when users see updates. Do not publicly cache private responses.
sections.visualNote: A new versioned file name lets the previous cache entry expire on its own.

lessons.title: SQL vs NoSQL
lessons.summary: Select a data model based on access patterns and guarantees.

sections.title: Model the data
sections.body: Relational databases organize data in tables and support joins and SQL. NoSQL databases include key-value, document, wide-column, and graph models.
sections.visualNote: Sketch how a single user operation reads or changes the data in each model.

sections.title: Compare guarantees
sections.body: Transactions, consistency, indexes, and scaling behavior vary by product. Check the actual guarantees instead of relying on the category name.
sections.visualNote: Compare the guarantees of the specific database and configuration.

sections.title: Start with queries
sections.body: List the reads, writes, constraints, and expected scale. Choose the simplest store that supports those needs and operational requirements.
sections.visualNote: Start with the reads and writes you need most often.

lessons.title: Indexes
lessons.summary: Trade write cost and storage for faster lookups.

sections.title: Find rows
sections.body: An index maintains an additional structure that helps a database locate matching rows without scanning every row.
sections.visualNote: An index can narrow the set of rows the database needs to examine.

sections.title: Match the query
sections.body: Column order, selectivity, and query predicates affect whether an index is useful. Inspect the query plan and measure real workloads.
sections.visualNote: Test with representative data. A planner can select a scan when a query matches many rows.

sections.title: Pay the write cost
sections.body: Inserts and updates must maintain indexes. Extra indexes consume storage and can slow writes.
sections.visualNote: Keep an index when the read benefit justifies its storage and write costs.

lessons.title: Storage Engines
lessons.summary: Compare common read and write paths.

sections.title: B-tree storage
sections.body: B-trees keep keys ordered in pages. They support efficient point lookups and range scans, with updates to pages on disk.
sections.visualNote: The engine reads pages from disk on a cache miss and writes modified pages back. The two arrows show these directions.

sections.title: Log-structured storage
sections.body: An LSM tree buffers writes and persists sorted files. Background compaction merges those files and reclaims obsolete data.
sections.visualNote: The arrow to Disk represents a batch of sorted records. Background compaction reads and writes more data as it merges files.

sections.title: Consider amplification
sections.body: Storage engines trade read, write, and space amplification differently. Choose using the workload and the database's actual behavior.
sections.visualNote: Choose with the expected reads and writes. Measure extra I/O and disk space under that workload.

lessons.title: Replication
lessons.summary: Keep copies of data to improve availability and read capacity.

sections.title: Copy writes
sections.body: A primary accepts writes and sends changes to replicas. Readers may use replicas when their consistency requirements allow it.
sections.visualNote: Each read needs a destination that meets its freshness requirement.

sections.title: Account for lag
sections.body: With asynchronous replication a replica can be behind the primary. A user may not immediately see a write they just made.
sections.visualNote: Send a read that must see a recent write to a sufficiently up-to-date copy.

sections.title: Recover from failure
sections.body: Failover promotes another replica, but the system must prevent conflicting primaries and account for writes that were not replicated.
sections.visualNote: Prevent the old primary from accepting new writes after the new primary takes over.

lessons.title: Sharding
lessons.summary: Partition a dataset across multiple machines.

sections.title: Choose a key
sections.body: A shard key determines where a record lives. Pick a key that distributes load and supports the most important queries.
sections.visualNote: Pick a key that sends common operations to a small set of partitions.

sections.title: Route operations
sections.body: The router uses the shard key to select a partition. Queries without the key may need to contact many shards.
sections.visualNote: If the router cannot derive the key, it may need to query several partitions.

sections.title: Handle hotspots
sections.body: Uneven keys can overload one shard. Resharding and cross-shard transactions introduce operational complexity.
sections.visualNote: Measure requests per shard. A few popular keys can overload one shard even with even data sizes.

lessons.title: Consistent Hashing
lessons.summary: Reduce key movement when the number of nodes changes.

sections.title: Place keys on a ring
sections.body: Hash both keys and nodes onto a ring. Assign each key to the next node in a chosen direction.
sections.visualNote: The same key maps to the same owner while the ring stays the same.

sections.title: Add a node
sections.body: Adding or removing a node changes ownership for part of the ring instead of remapping every key.
sections.visualNote: Only keys in the new node’s acquired interval move under simple ring placement.

sections.title: Balance the load
sections.body: Virtual nodes can improve distribution, but a hot key can still overload its owner. Measure skew and plan replication separately.
sections.visualNote: More positions can balance ownership without splitting requests for one popular key.

lessons.title: Unique IDs at Scale
lessons.summary: Generate identifiers without a single bottleneck.

sections.title: Define requirements
sections.body: Decide whether identifiers must be globally unique, sortable, compact, or hard to guess. These properties are different.
sections.visualNote: Decide whether the identifier will appear in a user-facing URL or stay internal.

sections.title: Generate IDs
sections.body: Random UUIDs avoid central coordination with a very low collision probability. Time-based schemes can improve ordering but require careful clock and node handling.
sections.visualNote: Time-based formats need a design for clock changes and concurrent writers.

sections.title: Check the trade-offs
sections.body: Identifier shape affects index locality and information disclosure. Do not treat a predictable identifier as an authorization control.
sections.visualNote: Authorize each request independently of whether a client can guess the ID.

lessons.title: CAP & Consistency
lessons.summary: Understand availability and consistency during a network partition.

sections.title: A partition occurs
sections.body: A network partition prevents nodes from communicating reliably. Replicas must decide how to handle requests while communication is impaired.
sections.visualNote: This example assumes requests can still reach both sides of the partition.

sections.title: Choose behavior
sections.body: During a partition, a system cannot guarantee both availability for every request and linearizable consistency. The choice depends on the operation and guarantees.
sections.visualNote: Set the failure behavior per operation. A stale response can be acceptable for some reads.

sections.title: Resolve changes
sections.body: Weaker consistency can allow replicas to diverge temporarily. Define how conflicts are detected and resolved after communication returns.
sections.visualNote: State how to handle updates accepted on both sides before the link recovered.

lessons.title: Consensus & Leaders
lessons.summary: Coordinate a replicated state machine across failures.

sections.title: Elect a leader
sections.body: Consensus protocols such as Raft elect a leader to coordinate changes among a group of replicas.
sections.visualNote: A majority requirement prevents two disjoint groups from electing different leaders for the same term.

sections.title: Commit a change
sections.body: The leader replicates a proposed log entry. A quorum must accept it before it is committed under the protocol's rules.
sections.visualNote: The leader waits for the required replicas before it reports a committed change.

sections.title: Handle failure
sections.body: If the leader fails, a new leader can be elected by a quorum. Losing a quorum prevents progress until enough members recover.
sections.visualNote: If too few replicas remain reachable, operations that need agreement must wait.

lessons.title: Transactions & Isolation
lessons.summary: Keep related changes correct under concurrent access.

sections.title: Group changes
sections.body: A transaction groups operations so they can commit or roll back together. The exact guarantees depend on the database and configuration.
sections.visualNote: Use one transaction for changes that must take effect together.

sections.title: Control concurrency
sections.body: Isolation levels define which concurrent effects a transaction can observe. Lower isolation can allow anomalies such as non-repeatable reads.
sections.visualNote: Repeat the same read inside two concurrent transactions to test the visible behavior.

sections.title: Choose and test
sections.body: Use constraints and a suitable isolation level for the invariant. Handle retries for conflicts and serialization failures.
sections.visualNote: On a serialization failure, retry the whole transaction with a bound.

lessons.title: Files & Media
lessons.summary: Store large objects separately from application metadata.

sections.title: Upload a file
sections.body: Object storage holds file bytes while a database stores metadata and references. Direct uploads can reduce load on application servers.
sections.visualNote: Publish the file reference when the corresponding object is ready.

sections.title: Serve the file
sections.body: A CDN can cache public media. Private files need authorization and short-lived access where appropriate.
sections.visualNote: Check authorization before you issue a link to a private file.

sections.title: Process safely
sections.body: Validate uploads, limit size, and process media asynchronously when required. Plan lifecycle and cleanup for orphaned objects.
sections.visualNote: Use separate states for uploaded and ready so readers know when they can use the file.

lessons.title: REST, RPC & GraphQL
lessons.summary: Compare ways services expose operations and data.

sections.title: Choose a contract
sections.body: REST commonly exposes resources over HTTP, RPC exposes operations, and GraphQL lets clients request fields through a schema.
sections.visualNote: Compare how a client would make the same request with each interface.

sections.title: Plan evolution
sections.body: Define schemas, error behavior, pagination, and compatibility. Protect clients when fields or operations change.
sections.visualNote: Add a new field before you remove one that deployed clients still use.

sections.title: Operate the API
sections.body: Authentication, authorization, timeouts, rate limits, and observability apply regardless of the API style.
sections.visualNote: Apply authentication and rate limits at the entry point and authorization where the action is enforced.

lessons.title: Message Queues
lessons.summary: Decouple work from the request path.

sections.title: Enqueue work
sections.body: A producer places a job on a queue so a worker can process it later. This can absorb bursts and shorten the request path.
sections.visualNote: Track the oldest queued job to see when workers fall behind.

sections.title: Process reliably
sections.body: A worker acknowledges successful work. If delivery is at least once, duplicates can occur, so handlers should be idempotent.
sections.visualNote: Make the job safe to run again if the worker finishes but loses its acknowledgment.

sections.title: Handle failures
sections.body: Use bounded retries and a dead-letter path for jobs that repeatedly fail. Monitor queue age as well as queue depth.
sections.visualNote: Keep enough context to investigate a failed job before you replay it.

lessons.title: Pub/Sub & Events
lessons.summary: Send events to multiple independent consumers.

sections.title: Publish an event
sections.body: A producer publishes an event describing something that happened. Multiple subscribers can react without direct calls from the producer.
sections.visualNote: Each subscriber can handle a different task triggered by the same event.

sections.title: Design the event
sections.body: Give events stable identifiers and versioned schemas. Include the data consumers need while avoiding unnecessary sensitive data.
sections.visualNote: Avoid requiring every subscriber to upgrade when a publisher adds a field.

sections.title: Expect duplicates
sections.body: Delivery order and duplication depend on the broker. Make consumers idempotent and define replay and retention policies.
sections.visualNote: Use event IDs and the broker’s ordering guarantees to handle repeated delivery.

lessons.title: Real-time Updates
lessons.summary: Deliver changes to clients with an appropriate connection model.

sections.title: Poll for changes
sections.body: Polling is simple but can waste requests or delay updates. The interval sets a trade-off between freshness and load.
sections.visualNote: A shorter interval reduces wait time and increases request volume.

sections.title: Keep a connection
sections.body: Server-sent events stream server-to-client updates; WebSockets support bidirectional messages. Both require connection management.
sections.visualNote: Use a bidirectional connection when the client and server both need to send updates independently.

sections.title: Recover after disconnect
sections.body: Clients should reconnect and recover missed updates using sequence numbers or a fresh snapshot when the protocol supports it.
sections.visualNote: If missed updates are no longer available, fetch a fresh snapshot.

lessons.title: Redundancy & Failover
lessons.summary: Reduce the effect of component failures.

sections.title: Remove single points
sections.body: Replicate critical components across independent failure domains. A second instance only helps if it does not share the same failure cause.
sections.visualNote: Place the standby where a failure of the primary is less likely to affect it.

sections.title: Detect and fail over
sections.body: Health checks and failover mechanisms redirect work after a failure. Detection, promotion, and recovery all take time.
sections.visualNote: Separate failure detection time from the time it takes to route requests again.

sections.title: Test recovery
sections.body: Measure recovery time and data loss against objectives. Exercise failover and restore procedures before an incident.
sections.visualNote: Run a failover exercise with a workload that resembles normal traffic.

lessons.title: Rate Limiting
lessons.summary: Protect finite capacity by controlling request rates.

sections.title: Set a limit
sections.body: A rate limiter applies a policy to an identity or resource, such as requests per user per minute.
sections.visualNote: Set the scope based on the resource to protect. A per-user limit and a service-wide limit protect different resources.

sections.title: Choose an algorithm
sections.body: Token buckets allow controlled bursts. Fixed and sliding windows have different accuracy and storage costs.
sections.visualNote: A token bucket can allow a short burst when tokens have accumulated.

sections.title: Return useful feedback
sections.body: Reject excess requests with a clear response and retry guidance. Distributed limiters must account for shared state and failure behavior.
sections.visualNote: Return retry guidance when the service knows when the caller can try again.

lessons.title: Timeouts & Retries
lessons.summary: Bound waiting and avoid amplifying failures.

sections.title: Set a deadline
sections.body: A timeout bounds how long a caller waits. Set a deadline appropriate to the user request and downstream work.
sections.visualNote: Give downstream calls enough time to finish within the caller’s remaining deadline.

sections.title: Retry carefully
sections.body: Retry only suitable failures, with bounded attempts, backoff, and jitter. A timeout does not prove the original operation failed.
sections.visualNote: Retry short-lived failures only while enough time remains for another attempt.

sections.title: Prevent duplicate effects
sections.body: Use idempotent operations or idempotency keys when retrying writes. Limit retries so an overloaded dependency can recover.
sections.visualNote: A timeout leaves the outcome uncertain. A stable key can let the server recognize another attempt at the same operation.

lessons.title: Observability
lessons.summary: Use metrics, logs, and traces to understand system behavior.

sections.title: Measure symptoms
sections.body: Metrics show trends in latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. Define service-level indicators from the user's perspective.
sections.visualNote: Measure the rate of failed and slow requests from the caller’s point of view.

sections.title: Follow a request
sections.body: Distributed traces connect work across services. Structured logs add context for investigation while avoiding secrets.
sections.visualNote: Follow the same request across components to see where it waited.

sections.title: Act on signals
sections.body: Alert on actionable symptoms and use dashboards to investigate causes. Test that telemetry remains useful during failures.
sections.visualNote: Alert on a symptom that needs a response. Use traces and logs to investigate it.

lessons.title: Monolith vs Microservices
lessons.summary: Choose service boundaries based on real needs.

sections.title: Start with boundaries
sections.body: A modular monolith deploys as one unit. Microservices deploy separately and communicate over a network.
sections.visualNote: Module boundaries make it possible to understand the responsibilities inside a single deployment.

sections.title: Compare costs
sections.body: Independent deployment and scaling can help teams, but distributed services add network failures, data coordination, and operational work.
sections.visualNote: Independent releases add network timeouts, service monitoring, and data coordination.

sections.title: Evolve deliberately
sections.body: Define clear domain boundaries first. Split a service when the benefits justify the added complexity.
sections.visualNote: A team can extract a part that needs its own release cycle or scaling policy.

lessons.title: Service Discovery
lessons.summary: Find healthy service instances as they change.

sections.title: Register instances
sections.body: Instances advertise their locations through a registry or platform service. Registration must be kept current as instances change.
sections.visualNote: Remove instances that can no longer serve traffic.

sections.title: Resolve a destination
sections.body: A client or proxy discovers available instances and selects one. DNS and platform service discovery are common approaches.
sections.visualNote: The caller or proxy selects a healthy endpoint from the available addresses.

sections.title: Handle stale results
sections.body: Health checks, expiration, and retries help when an address is stale. The discovery mechanism itself must remain available.
sections.visualNote: Refresh the list when a selected endpoint no longer accepts connections.

lessons.title: Sagas & Distributed Tx
lessons.summary: Use a saga to coordinate a distributed transaction across services.

sections.title: Break work into steps
sections.body: A saga coordinates local transactions across services. Each step commits independently instead of using one database transaction.
sections.visualNote: Each service commits its own change. Keep the outcome of each step so a retry can continue safely.

sections.title: Compensate failures
sections.body: If a later step fails, compensating actions can undo earlier business effects where possible. Compensation is not always an exact rollback.
sections.visualNote: A refund is a new action with its own result. Record its success or failure.

sections.title: Make progress visible
sections.body: Persist workflow state, handle duplicate messages, and provide a way to inspect and recover stuck workflows.
sections.visualNote: Store the current step so an operator can tell which actions still need attention.

lessons.title: Batch & Stream Processing
lessons.summary: Choose how and when to process incoming data.

sections.title: Process in batches
sections.body: Batch processing handles a bounded set of data on a schedule. It is useful when results do not need to be immediate.
sections.visualNote: Choose a batch when the result can wait until the next scheduled run.

sections.title: Process a stream
sections.body: Stream processing handles events continuously and can reduce result delay. It must account for late events, state, and recovery.
sections.visualNote: Define how late events affect results that may already have been published.

sections.title: Define correctness
sections.body: Choose acceptable latency, ordering, and duplicate behavior. Validate that replay and checkpointing meet the use case.
sections.visualNote: Test recovery with the same inputs to check whether it changes the result.

lessons.title: Authentication
lessons.summary: Verify who is making a request.

sections.title: Verify identity
sections.body: Authentication establishes an identity using credentials or an identity provider. Use established protocols and libraries.
sections.visualNote: An application can delegate login to an identity provider and verify its response.

sections.title: Maintain a session
sections.body: Sessions or tokens carry authentication state. Protect them in transit and apply suitable expiration and revocation rules.
sections.visualNote: Set a lifetime that matches the amount of time a session remains useful.

sections.title: Defend the entry point
sections.body: Use strong credential storage, rate limits, and multi-factor authentication where appropriate. Authentication alone does not grant access to every resource.
sections.visualNote: Use multiple factors where appropriate to limit the impact of a stolen password.

lessons.title: Authorization
lessons.summary: Decide which actions an identity may perform.

sections.title: Check the action
sections.body: Authorization decides whether an authenticated identity can perform an action on a particular resource.
sections.visualNote: A user who can update their own record may need separate permission to update someone else’s.

sections.title: Apply least privilege
sections.body: Grant only the permissions needed. Roles and attributes can express policies, but resource ownership still needs checking.
sections.visualNote: Keep permissions limited to the actions a role needs.

sections.title: Enforce on the server
sections.body: Check access at trusted boundaries on every relevant request. Client-side controls alone cannot enforce authorization.
sections.visualNote: Apply the policy at the trusted service before it reads or changes the resource.

lessons.title: Encryption & Secrets
lessons.summary: Protect data and manage keys separately from code.

sections.title: Protect data in transit
sections.body: TLS protects traffic between endpoints when configured and validated correctly. Encrypt sensitive data at rest according to its threat model.
sections.visualNote: Use TLS on connections that carry sensitive data and verify the endpoint identity.

sections.title: Manage secrets
sections.body: Store credentials in a managed secret store or another controlled mechanism. Do not commit them to source code or logs.
sections.visualNote: The service can retrieve its credential at runtime. Keep credential values out of logs and code.

sections.title: Rotate and audit
sections.body: Limit access to keys, plan rotation and revocation, and record access. Encryption does not replace authorization.
sections.visualNote: Verify that services can switch to a new key before you retire the old one.

lessons.title: Testing
lessons.summary: Verify behavior at the right levels.

sections.title: Test behavior
sections.body: Unit tests check focused behavior; integration tests verify boundaries such as database and API interactions.
sections.visualNote: Verify behavior at the layer where a failure is easiest to reproduce.

sections.title: Test the system
sections.body: End-to-end tests cover important user paths. Load and failure tests reveal behavior that small functional tests can miss.
sections.visualNote: Use load and failure tests when behavior depends on traffic or component outages.

sections.title: Keep feedback useful
sections.body: Choose a small set of reliable tests for critical risks. A passing test suite does not prove every production condition is safe.
sections.visualNote: Keep a failing check actionable by making its cause clear and repeatable.

lessons.title: CI/CD & Deployments
lessons.summary: Deliver changes with repeatable checks and recovery.

sections.title: Build and verify
sections.body: A pipeline builds an artifact and runs relevant checks for each change. The same artifact can move through deployment environments.
sections.visualNote: Promote the artifact that passed the checks so later stages run the tested build.

sections.title: Release gradually
sections.body: Rolling, blue-green, or canary releases can reduce the impact of a bad change. Each needs health checks and a clear rollback path.
sections.visualNote: Start with a small rollout. Use defined health signals to continue or roll back.

sections.title: Manage compatibility
sections.body: Database migrations and API changes must support old and new versions during a rollout. Monitor the service after deployment.
sections.visualNote: Keep the database and API compatible with both versions until the rollout ends.

lessons.title: HLD & LLD
lessons.summary: Move from requirements to components and detailed contracts.

sections.title: Clarify requirements
sections.body: Identify the users, key operations, constraints, and scale. State assumptions and ask which trade-offs matter most.
sections.visualNote: Write down the expected load and the user actions the system must support.

sections.title: Sketch the high-level design
sections.body: Show the major components, data flows, storage, and external dependencies. Explain why each is needed.
sections.visualNote: Trace a representative request through each component to see what it needs.

sections.title: Explore details
sections.body: Define key APIs, data models, failure cases, and bottlenecks. Use the remaining time to discuss the highest-risk decisions.
sections.visualNote: Specify the error and retry behavior for the most important operations.

lessons.title: Design a URL Shortener
lessons.summary: Design a service that creates and resolves short links.

sections.title: Define the contract
sections.body: Create a short link for a valid URL and redirect a visitor from the short code. Clarify expiration, custom aliases, and expected traffic.
sections.visualNote: Decide whether a short code can expire and whether callers can choose their own code.

sections.title: Store and resolve
sections.body: Generate a unique code and store its mapping to the destination. On a lookup, retrieve the mapping and return an appropriate redirect.
sections.visualNote: Use a temporary redirect when the service needs to keep control over destination changes.

sections.title: Scale and protect
sections.body: Cache popular mappings, partition by code when needed, and prevent abuse. Consider collision handling, availability, and deletion.
sections.visualNote: Partition by code when the store reaches its limit. Set cache freshness to match expiry and deletion.

lessons.title: Design a News Feed
lessons.summary: Combine posts into a feed that stays responsive at scale.

sections.title: Define the feed
sections.body: Clarify who sees a post, ordering, pagination, freshness, and traffic. Separate the write path from feed reads.
sections.visualNote: Decide whose posts can appear and how users page through the result.

sections.title: Choose fan-out
sections.body: Fan-out on write prepares feeds ahead of time; fan-out on read merges content when requested. Popular authors can make write fan-out expensive.
sections.visualNote: Preparing feeds on publish lowers read work but can create many writes for one popular author.

sections.title: Handle trade-offs
sections.body: A hybrid approach can treat very popular accounts differently. Consider ranking, caching, privacy changes, and stale results.
sections.visualNote: A hybrid design can prepare most feeds ahead of time and merge posts from high-fan-out authors at read time.

lessons.title: Design a Chat System
lessons.summary: Deliver messages reliably to online and offline users.

sections.title: Define the experience
sections.body: Clarify one-to-one or group chat, delivery guarantees, ordering, retention, and offline behavior.
sections.visualNote: State whether the system must preserve message order per conversation.

sections.title: Send and persist
sections.body: The service authenticates the sender, persists a message, and delivers it to connected recipients. Offline recipients can retrieve it later.
sections.visualNote: Persist the message so offline recipients can retrieve it on reconnect.

sections.title: Handle reconnects
sections.body: Use message IDs and acknowledgments to handle retries and duplicates. Define ordering scope and protect access to conversations.
sections.visualNote: Use the last acknowledged position to resume delivery and use message IDs to detect repeats.
